body.en: Jesus made Capernaum, a fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, the base of his Galilean ministry — Matthew calls it 'his own city'. Here he taught in the synagogue, healed Peter's mother-in-law, and called fishermen and a tax-collector to follow him.

The lake itself is the stage for much of the ministry: the calling of the first disciples, teaching from a boat, the calming of the storm, and the walking on the water. Its sudden squalls, dropping from the surrounding hills, frame several Gospel scenes.

Far to the north, at the pagan sanctuary of Caesarea Philippi by the springs of the Jordan, Peter confessed Jesus as the Messiah — the turning point after which Jesus began to teach plainly about his coming death in Jerusalem.

title.en: Paul's First Journey: Antioch to Galatia

body.en: The church at Syrian Antioch — where believers were first called 'Christians' — set apart Barnabas and Saul and sent them out. Antioch, not Jerusalem, becomes the launch-point of the Gentile mission.
At Paphos, the Roman capital of Cyprus, the pair confronted the magician Elymas before the proconsul Sergius Paulus. From this point Luke calls the apostle 'Paul' and treats him as the leader.

In the synagogue of Pisidian Antioch Paul preached his first recorded sermon, tracing Israel's history to Jesus. Welcomed, then opposed, he turned to the Gentiles — a pattern repeated across the journeys.

At Lystra a healing led the crowd to hail Paul and Barnabas as the gods Hermes and Zeus; soon after, hostile agitators stoned Paul and left him for dead. He recovered and pressed on to Derbe before retracing the route home.
